extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in technology policy, FCC rulemaking, and net neutrality
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing the integrity, provenance, and weight of public comments in administrative rulemaking (notice-and-comment) proceedings, with attention to fraud, astroturfing, disclosure, and agency safeguards. Focus is on detecting/managing large-scale fake comment campaigns in contexts like FCC net neutrality rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency use of comments to shape rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The agency is supposed to use the comments it receives, from industry and public-industry groups and the public, to shape how it makes its rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments submitted in a proceeding are part of the administrative record and should inform rulemaking decisions; therefore the provenance and reliability of those comments matter for policy outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity and attributable authorship of comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments should be authentic and attributable to real individuals who knowingly submitted them; fake or misattributed comments undermine the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Red flags include extremely large numbers of submissions traced to a single individual (e.g., one person submitting millions of comments), use of stolen identities, or mass submission patterns. The article cites a 19-year-old who submitted over 7.7 million comments and senators whose identities were stolen to file fake comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of sponsoring parties and industry involvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizers of comment campaigns should disclose industry funding and involvement rather than hide it to create an impression of grassroots support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Broadband for America campaign sought to make it seem like 'widespread grassroots support' while hiding broadband industry involvement; failure to disclose is criticized as 'troubling' and misleads agencies reviewing the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on raw volume alone (detect astroturfing)
rubrics_metrics.description: High volume of comments can be manufactured and therefore is an unreliable sole indicator of public sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 2017 proceeding had over 22 million comments but nearly 18 million were found to be fake; rulemakers should treat sheer comment counts with caution and look for signs of coordinated campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification of address/origin information
rubrics_metrics.description: Comment provenance should be consistent and credible (e.g., mailing addresses and geographic origin should be plausible for the claimed commenters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report noted a 'distinct group' of 1.6 million comments that used mailing addresses outside the U.S., which is a signal warranting further scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead generator and contractor integrity (consent and data source verification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Third-party firms that generate or submit comments must verify consent and source data; copying previously collected or stolen data is improper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The lead generators copied names and addresses they already had and claimed those people had agreed to join the campaign; one company copied information stolen in a data breach. Best practice: verify each submitter's informed consent and provenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency duty to detect problems and improve comment processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should detect widespread problems in the comment record and implement reforms to improve the commenting process and prevent fraud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acting FCC chairwoman Jessica Rosenworcel said 'widespread problems with the record' were troubling and that the agency 'has to learn and improve the commenting process.' Improvements could include better authentication, anomaly detection, and transparency measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement, remediation, and penalties for fraudulent campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: Actors responsible for generating fraudulent comments can be investigated, required to change practices, and subject to monetary penalties or settlements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New York AG agreements with Fluent Inc., Opt-Intelligence Inc., and React2Media Inc. require changes to future advocacy practices and $4.4 million in fines; law enforcement may continue investigating other responsible parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal liability linked to knowledge and due diligence
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil or criminal liability for organizations that benefit from fake comment campaigns may depend on whether they had direct knowledge of the fraud and on the sufficiency of their oversight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report said it had not found evidence that broadband companies had 'direct knowledge of fraud' and therefore did not conclude they violated New York law; organizations should perform due diligence and disclose involvement to avoid liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigative follow-up and attribution work
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-proceeding investigations are necessary to attribute responsibility for fake comments and to identify additional actors involved in manipulative campaigns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The attorney general's office and other law enforcement agencies continued investigating 'other responsible parties,' underscoring the importance of forensic analysis of submission patterns, data sources, and contractor relationships.
